issues.issue: Credit for returns is made to depend on "policies and standards set and established from time to time by COMPANY," which lets COMPANY alter DISTRIBUTOR's credit rights unilaterally notwithstanding Section 15(iii)'s requirement that modifications be by a signed writing. Whether such policies bind as contract terms is unresolved.

The proviso withholding the guarantee "where PRODUCTS are manufactured by DISTRIBUTOR and shipped under DISTRIBUTOR'S labels" cannot be squared with Section I(ii), which defines PRODUCTS as products COMPANY authorizes for sale to DISTRIBUTOR. The carve-out describes goods that cannot be PRODUCTS under the instrument's own definition.

The closing words forbid weakening COMPANY's "property rights in said registrations," but no registrations are identified anywhere in the Agreement — the defined term is "Trademarks," which includes unregistered names and logos. The antecedent failure leaves the scope of the covenant uncertain.

"COMPANY shall supply DISTRIBUTOR, at COMPANY'S sole discretion, with the following ... as may be available to COMPANY" states a mandatory duty and its own complete negation in one sentence. Whether any information or equipment is owed at all cannot be determined from the words.

COMPANY may "require and withhold from DISTRIBUTOR, a reasonable sum to assure return or replacement of equipment" without any cap, measure or mechanism for the withholding. What sum is "reasonable" and from what it may be withheld is left open.

The bar on DISTRIBUTOR using any "descriptive literature, advertising, etc., pertaining to PRODUCTS without COMPANY'S prior written consent" cannot be squared with Section 3(ii)(u), which makes DISTRIBUTOR "solely responsible for any and all promotions, sales and marketing programs, advertising and the like." Which provision governs DISTRIBUTOR's advertising is unresolved.
"[T]he General market information regarding the TERRITORY" is undefined and given no content, frequency or format. What DISTRIBUTOR must hand over on request is indeterminate.

The confidentiality obligation cross-references "Sections 10(i) and 10(i)" — the same subsection twice, apparently a typographical error for 10(ii) — and otherwise covers "any and all business and technical information" without exclusions or a time limit. The scope of protected information is left unclear by the defective reference and the unbounded description.

"[A] change in COMPANY's business that results in COMPANY no longer using Independent DSDD distributors in this territory" is undefined as to what counts as "no longer using" and what "this territory" is measured against (Exhibit A, or some larger area). Whether a shift to a different distribution model triggers this ground is exactly what the words do not resolve.

This provision permits ninety-day termination only "for good cause" (defined as an uncured breach) or on a change in COMPANY's business, whereas Section 2 says that after December 31, 2008 "this agreement may be terminated by either party upon ninety (90) days written notice" with no cause requirement. The two cannot both be given effect.

Ground (a) permits immediate termination for an attempted transfer without consent "which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld," while Section 15(ii)(a) declares any attempted assignment void and a material breach and lets COMPANY reject an assignee by its own standards. The two treat the same conduct on inconsistent terms.

The clause gives "five (5) business days written notice" to cure and then measures forfeiture by "said five (5) day period," so the cure period is stated twice in inconsistent units. The mismatch changes how long DISTRIBUTOR actually has to cure.

The parenthetical exempting "DISTRIBUTOR'S isolated, but not systemic, curable failures to remove out-of-date merchandise" from immediate termination unless they occur six times in twelve months uses undefined terms ("isolated," "systemic") and is dropped mid-proviso. How it interacts with the two-failure rule in the same sentence is not determinable from the words.

The repurchase right is optional and confined to PRODUCTS "commercially usable or saleable with at least sixty (60) days of code fife remaining," a garbled and undefined measure that also leaves unsalable and short-coded stock with DISTRIBUTOR. What inventory qualifies on termination is uncertain.

The sentence bars "consequential, punitive or incidental damages" and then qualifies the bar with "in any cumulative amount greater than the sum of 50% of DISTRIBUTOR'S aggregate gross sales," so it reads both as an exclusion and as a cap. Whether it forbids such damages outright, caps them, or caps all damages on termination is unresolved on its face.

The grant of a security interest in "all PRODUCTS and related items ... in DISTRIBUTOR'S possession" with irrevocable self-help entry cannot easily be squared with Section 4(iii), under which PRODUCTS are "sold to DISTRIBUTOR absolutely" with title passing on delivery. The extent of COMPANY's retained rights in delivered goods is left to be worked out.

The two-year limit runs from when "the harm that gave rise to the cause of action arose," a trigger different from accrual or discovery and undefined for continuing or repeated breaches. When the clock starts on a claim such as wrongful termination or withheld credits is exactly what the words leave open.

A mutual indemnity for losses "caused ... by a breach of this Agreement" cannot readily be squared with Section 12(v), which bars or caps damages arising by reason of termination or expiration of the Agreement. Whether indemnity recovery escapes that limitation is unresolved.

The provision opens with a duty on "each party" to maintain insurance but the schedule of coverages, the excess layer and the certificate requirement are drafted only against DISTRIBUTOR. Whether COMPANY owes the same limits and proof of coverage is left ambiguous by the shift in subject.

The clause grants a right "in its sole discretion, to inspect, copy, and audit all such records" while in the same sentence "acknowledging that access to accounting and purchasing records shall be limited to services performed for COMPANY." The grant and the limitation contradict each other as to records covering DISTRIBUTOR's other product lines.

Notice may be given by personal service, courier, registered mail or facsimile, but the effectiveness sentence fixes the date only for notice "by mail, if sent only by mail service, or facsimile." When personally served or couriered notice — the method likely used for a ninety-day termination — takes effect is not stated.

Declaring every attempted assignment "void and without effect" and a material breach cannot be squared with the following paragraph and Section 12(ii)(a), which promise that consent will not be unreasonably withheld or delayed. Whether DISTRIBUTOR has a real, enforceable right to transfer is left in doubt.

COMPANY promises not to "unreasonably withhold or delay consent" but is then permitted to reject an assignee "according to COMPANY's standards for evaluating prospective distributors" and to impose conditions "among other requirements," so the reasonableness standard has no content. Whether any refusal could be unreasonable is the open question.

Permitting DISTRIBUTOR to conduct business through subdistributors cannot be squared with Section 3(ii)(a)(iii)A, which forbids "Wholesaler operations whereby 'in-store service' is not provided to individual store outlets," and with Section 15(ii)(a)'s bar on transferring the Agreement "in whole or in part." How far the subdistributor permission goes is unresolved.

COMPANY's freedom to assign to any affiliate, subsidiary, parent or division without consent stands against Section 15(ii)(a)'s premise that the distributorship is personal and non-transferable, and it does not say whether COMPANY remains liable after assignment. Whether an assignment releases COMPANY is left open.

Requiring modification "only by a written instrument duly executed by the parties" cannot be squared with Sections 3(ii)(b), 3(ii)(c) and 4(ii), which let COMPANY alter policies, revise Exhibit "B" "without notice ... in the sole discretion of COMPANY," and change prices and terms unilaterally. Which mechanism governs a change to DISTRIBUTOR's obligations is unresolved.

Delaware law is chosen for an agreement performed in New York by a New York distributor, while Section 12(vi) invokes "the Uniform Commercial Code" without identifying a state's enactment. Which body of law governs the security interest and self-help repossession is left unsettled.

The merger clause cancels prior agreements "except as otherwise expressly provided herein" while Section 2 contemplates a chain of successor DSDD Agreements — and the 2009 DSDD Agreement between the same parties contains the identical clause. Which agreement governs conduct and claims spanning both instruments is exactly what these words leave unresolved.

"[E]ach of which shall be deemed the original" (rather than "an original") is a mechanical error that, read literally, makes every counterpart the single original. The slip is small but changes the sense of the sentence.

The territory designation is a handwritten entry rendered as "Wy {NY Sn re ccluding all customers and channels of trade set forth on attached Exhibit B," so the geographic scope of the TERRITORY is illegible and indeterminate. Since Section I(iii) defines TERRITORY solely by reference to this exhibit, the central operative term has no ascertainable content.

The exclusions are stated as broad category labels illustrated by "e.g." examples ("Mass merchandisers (e.g., Target and Wal-Mart)"; "Specialty stores"; "Chain Warehouse programs"), so whether an unnamed retailer falls in an excluded category is a matter of construction. The Kmart carve-out inside the mass-merchandiser exclusion shows the categories do not stand on their own terms.

This grandfather permission to keep selling to existing customers "who fall within the above schedule" cannot be squared with Section 3(ii)(c)'s flat prohibition on selling to Exhibit "B" customers and channels, or with Section 12(iii)(a), which makes selling outside the AUTHORIZED CHANNEL OF TRADE a termination ground. Which text governs a legacy excluded-channel customer is the open question.

The recital that "there exists no relationship of any kind, contractual or otherwise" between the subdistributor and Kellogg sits against Section 15(ii)(a), which requires each subdistributor to execute and return this very undertaking to COMPANY, and against Exhibit C §7, which gives its terms overriding force. Whether the executed Exhibit C itself creates a direct relationship is left in doubt.

The covenant forbids any act or omission having a weakening effect "as determined by Kellogg in its sole and absolute discretion," so the breach standard is whatever Kellogg says it is. What conduct actually violates the section is not ascertainable from the words.

Kellogg's freedom to sell directly to the subdistributor's customers is qualified by "to the extent permitted by the agreement then in effect between Kellogg and Premier," a limit the subdistributor cannot see and which Sections 3(ii)(d) and 3(ii)(j) leave essentially unlimited. What the qualifier adds, if anything, requires reading both instruments together.

"[T]he goods constitution Products" is a garbled phrase, and the acknowledgment covers Kellogg or Premier altering or terminating "the business relationship between thern" without identifying which relationship. The mechanical errors obscure what is being waived.

The disclaimer of third-party beneficiary status sits against Exhibit C §7, which gives these terms priority over the subdistributor's own agreement with Premier, and against Section 15(ii)(a), which makes execution of this document a condition of the subdistribution. Whether the subdistributor has any enforceable standing under the Kellogg–Premier Agreement is left unclear.

The operative words are garbled and the sentence is truncated ("in its sole and absolute isoret fon expanding and/or otherwise increasing Kellogg's potential liability with respect to Pr"), so the prohibition has no complete predicate. What the subdistributor is forbidden to do cannot be read off the text.

The priority rule addresses only inconsistencies with "any agreement between Ind.Distr. and Premier" and says nothing about conflicts with the Kellogg–Premier Distributor Agreement, whose Section 15(vii) declares itself the entire agreement. The order of precedence between Exhibit C and the main Agreement is therefore unresolved.
